Let's walk through a real redemption so you can see exactly what this looks like in practice.

The Route: Newly introduced York JFK → Frankfurt FRA, nonstop The Aircraft: Lufthansa Boeing 747-8, upper deck business class The Cash Price: $6,500 (a realistic peak-season transatlantic business class fare) The Points Cost: 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles Out-of-Pocket Fees: ~$85 in government taxes CPP Achieved: 10.3 cents per point.

You've transferred 63,000 Citi ThankYou points to LifeMiles — instantly — spotted the award space on United.com the morning it opened, called LifeMiles to confirm, and had your booking locked in within 90 minutes of finding the seat.

Industry observers note that lufthansa's 747-8 upper deck business class is one of the most iconic products in commercial aviation. The upper deck seats — in a 2-2-2 configuration — sit quieter and smoother than the main deck, with fewer passengers and a more intimate cabin feel.

Your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet. You'll have direct aisle access (depending on your seat selection), a large personal entertainment screen, and Lufthansa's catering, which consistently ranks among the top transatlantic carriers. The meal service on JFK–FRA is legitimate: a proper multi-course dinner, a breakfast service as you approach Germany, and a snack menu available throughout.

Before you board, you'll have access to Lufthansa's business class lounge at JFK — typically the Lufthansa Business Lounge or, depending on timing, the partner lounge. Hot food, showers, and a genuine departure experience that costs nothing beyond the taxes you've already paid.

The flight itself is roughly 7.5 hours. In a flat bed, that's a real night's sleep — or close enough. You arrive in Frankfurt rested, which matters whether you're connecting onward or starting your trip immediately.

For the ChooseFI community: this is the redemption that pays for the honeymoon, the milestone anniversary trip, or the family adventure you've been planning since you first discovered travel rewards. The $6,500 you didn't spend stays in your index funds.

Book at the 355-day mark for peak dates. Lufthansa releases a small number of partner award seats when the schedule opens. The travelers who get summer business class awards are almost always the ones who searched on day 355. Set a calendar alert. Be ready.

According to recent reports, use Citi ThankYou for time-sensitive bookings. Because Citi transfers to LifeMiles are instant, you can find award space and complete your booking in a single session. This matters when you're racing to secure a specific seat before someone else grabs it.

Watch for LifeMiles purchased miles promotions. If you're 10,000–15,000 miles short of a redemption, purchasing miles during a 100% bonus promotion can effectively cost you 0.5–0.7 cents per mile — still leaving you with excellent overall CPP on the redemption. Check lifemiles.com regularly or set a Google Alert for "LifeMiles promotion.".

Industry observers note that verify your booking on the operating carrier's website. After booking through LifeMiles, always look up your PNR on lufthansa.com or swiss.com. If it appears correctly, your seat is real. If it doesn't, call LifeMiles immediately.

Search Swiss as an alternative to Lufthansa. Swiss International Air Lines is also a Star Alliance member, also bookable through LifeMiles at the same rates, and also operates excellent business class products on transatlantic routes. Swiss often has more partner award availability than Lufthansa on certain dates.

In a recent development, never transfer points before confirming availability. This is the most common — and most expensive — mistake in travel rewards. LifeMiles does not allow re-transfers out of the program.

Recent findings suggest that don't ignore the miles expiry policy. LifeMiles expire 12 months from your last earning activity. Any account activity — earning miles, purchasing miles, even a credit card transaction — resets the clock on your entire balance. Set a recurring reminder every 10 months to run a small transaction if you're holding a balance without an imminent booking.

Don't book Lufthansa First Class expecting the same experience. Lufthansa's First Class is a separate product with separate availability and pricing. Business class is the sweet spot here — outstanding value, more seats, and significantly better availability.

Recent findings suggest that avoid mixing Marriott Bonvoy transfers with tight timelines. At 3:1 and 1–5 days transfer time, Bonvoy is the slowest and least efficient path into LifeMiles. Initiative accordingly.

It has been revealed that this redemption is built for the experienced FI traveler who has already earned their first free night or domestic flight and is ready to graduate to aspirational international business class. You don't need to fly business class constantly — but for a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or a long-planned European trip, this is the redemption that makes the experience extraordinary without derailing your savings rate.

This is NOT the right redemption if:.

You need 63,000 LifeMiles per person, per direction. A couple flying one-way needs 126,000 miles. Most people will get there through a combination of one or two travel credit card welcome bonuses and organic spending — entirely achievable within the FI community's existing card strategy.

Industry observers note that ## Rated: Hard — Here's Why This redemption earns its **hard** rating from three compounding challenges, none of which is insurmountable but all of which require deliberate effort. **Challenge 1: Award Availability Is Limited.** Lufthansa releases partner award seats conservatively. You may search for weeks before finding space on your preferred route and dates. This isn't a redemption where you decide Tuesday you want to go and book Thursday. You need a booking window of weeks to months, and flexibility in your travel dates helps enormously. **Challenge 2: The Booking Process Has Friction.** LifeMiles' website doesn't always surface partner award availability accurately. You'll likely need to search on United.com to find the space, then call LifeMiles to actually book it. That phone call requires patience — hold times vary, and you'll need to clearly communicate flight numbers, dates, and cabin class to the agent. **Challenge 3: Timing the Transfer Is High-Stakes.** Because you can't transfer points *out* of LifeMiles, you're committing your points the moment you initiate a transfer. Finding the seat, moving the miles, and completing the booking requires confidence and speed. ## How to Overcome the Challenges 1. **Start searching early** — 300+ days out for peak travel. Use ExpertFlyer alerts to monitor availability passively. 2. **Use Citi ThankYou for instant transfers** so you can act immediately when you find a seat. 3. **Practice the phone booking process** once before your high-stakes redemption — call LifeMiles with a simple question to understand their system. If you've successfully booked one or two simpler awards before, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has members completing this redemption every year — and every single one says the boarding moment made the effort completely worth it.

Sources indicate that united demonstrates Star Alliance partner availability that LifeMiles can book. Search for Saver-level awards in business or first class on your target route. Note the exact carrier, flight number, and date.

In a recent development, amex MR, Chase UR, Citi ThankYou, and Capital One miles all transfer to LifeMiles. Amex transfers are often fastest (same day). Transfer only after confirming availability in Step 2.

It has been revealed that premium cabin award space is limited and competitive. Once your transferred miles appear in your LifeMiles account, complete the booking immediately. Do not wait — the seat can be taken by another searcher.

It has been revealed that lifeMiles charges low taxes and fees on most partner awards, typically $30-$100 depending on the route. Some carriers (notably British Airways) add fuel surcharges, but most Star Alliance carriers keep fees minimal through LifeMiles.

It has been revealed that yes, Lufthansa First Class is bookable through LifeMiles at 87,000 miles one-way from the US to Europe. Availability is limited and typically released at 14 days before departure for partner programs, though some space appears further out. Search on United.com first to confirm Lufthansa First saver space exists before transferring.

Transfer times vary by partner. Amex Membership Rewards transfers often post same-day. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers typically take 1-2 business days. Citi ThankYou and Capital One transfers can take 1-3 days. Always account for transfer time when booking time-sensitive award space.

According to recent reports, most Star Alliance carriers booked through LifeMiles have low or no fuel surcharges. The notable exception is British Airways (a oneworld carrier, not bookable through LifeMiles). Taxes and fees on typical Star Alliance routes run $30-$100 per ticket, making LifeMiles one of the cheapest programs for out-of-pocket award costs.

Sources indicate that if the booking fails because award space disappeared between your search and transfer, the miles sit in your LifeMiles account. They do not expire as long as you have account activity every 12 months. You can use them for a future booking, but you cannot transfer them back to your original program.

In a recent development, this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

In a recent development, avianca LifeMiles is the program that lets FI-community travelers fly the same premium cabins as frequent business travelers at a fraction of the points cost. By consistently underpricing Star Alliance awards, LifeMiles turns 63,000-87,000 transferable points into experiences worth $8,000 or more. The process requires discipline (never transfer before confirming availability), patience (searching for saver space takes time), and a willingness to navigate a less polished booking experience. But the value is real: 15-20 cents per point on aspirational flights that would be unreachable at cash prices.

Read on to learn the best ways to earn cash without a regular 9-5 job, plus tips on how almost anyone can get started.

Plus, they can hire and fire clients based on their personal needs and preferences, and their income potential is unlimited. According to ZipRecruiter, freelancers in the U.S. average $63.53 per hour.

Investing in dividend stocks is one of the best ways to earn money without a regular job. Many early retirees find a way to live and pay bills based solely on the dividends they receive from various stocks.

You can make money driving for Uber or Lyft on your own time, picking and choosing the days and hours you want to work.

Not only is rideshare work one of the most flexible side hustles, but you can earn $20 per hour and more with tips.

If you are low on free time but still want to make money without a job, consider selling stuff you don’t need. An array of online platforms makes it a breeze, although some platforms work better for selling.

For example, you can use Poshmark to earn money selling used clothing and accessories, while used electronics tend to sell best on platforms like eBay.com, Decluttr, BuyBackWorld, and Gazelle.

If you have home decor, furniture, or workout equipment to sell, you’ll almost always do better unloading those items locally on Facebook Marketplace.

Recent findings suggest that starting a YouTube channel is another way to earn money without a job, but that doesn’t mean it’s not work. The fact is, that creating quality videos and building an audience takes a lot of creativity and time. Plus, not everyone who tries to build a YouTube channel will succeed.

That remarked, you can earn income without a regular job. I know because I have done it with my YouTube channel, Wealth Hacker.

How much you can earn on YouTube varies quite a bit, but it’s possible to earn thousands of dollars per month. If you’re curious about monetizing videos, my in-depth guide will show you how to make money on YouTube.

Sources indicate that donating plasma is a unique way to earn money without a job, although it’s not very glamorous. DonatingPlasma.org makes it easy to find plasma donation centers in your area, and you can earn as much as $100 for your first donation.

Recent findings suggest that that said, subsequent plasma donations typically earn closer to $50. You’ll also be limited by the number of times you can donate plasma within a month. However, it’s possible to use this side gig to earn an extra $500 per month, which you can use to supplement your primary income.

Sources indicate that if you are willing to complete various tasks that help regular workers do their jobs, consider becoming a crowd worker. This gig will have you finishing up to-do lists of jobs that don’t require specific technical skills.

For example, you may get paid to proofread documents, label images, revision a resume, complete a form, or complete a data entry assignment.

Several platforms help you find crowd-working gigs, but the best ones include Microworkers and Clickworker.

If you want to do something simple that will get you moving, consider delivering groceries using apps like Instacart or Shipt. You get paid hourly, plus tips and all you have to do is head to the store, purchase groceries according to a list, and deliver them to people in your neighborhood.

The gig is extremely flexible, similar to driving for Uber or Lyft.

Sources indicate that another non-job gig lets you get paid to deliver packages for Amazon.com. You can do this through a platform called Amazon Flex, which promises its drivers anywhere from $18 to $25 per hour.

Unlike a regular Amazon job, Flex lets you pick the day and the hours you want to work. To get started, you need to create a free account, get approved, and start reserving blocks of time you want to deliver packages.

Finally, you can earn money by selling unwanted or unused gift cards in your possession. This hustle is made easy thanks to platforms like GiftDeals.com and CardCash.com.

According to recent reports, you won’t get the total value of your gift cards, but you should get 90% or more of the gift card balance for each card you sell. While selling gift cards for less than their total value may not seem ideal, it’s better than not using them and getting nothing in return.

Finally, you can earn small amounts of money by signing up with the best online survey sites. Not only is this side hustle as easy as it gets, but you can participate and get paid during your spare time and even on your phone.

Other online survey sites to check out include the following:.

There you have it, 26 ways to make money without a job. While many of the jobs on our list won’t replace your 9-5, they can be a great way to increase your income so you can pay off debt or break the cycle of living paycheck to paycheck.

#79646. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2040 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun latest way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,.

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

In a recent development, so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

Sources indicate that one of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

In a recent development, I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

It has been revealed that during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Industry observers note that then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

Recent findings suggest that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

Industry observers note that it reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Sources indicate that experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

It has been revealed that one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

In a recent development, and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

It has been revealed that but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

In a recent development, as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

*(Vine Gold is not all that useful as it turns out as 99.9% of the available items seem to be the same trinkets you see in the Silver tier).

** What about the Heated Vest that started it all? Well, I still love that thing and now that fall is coming back it is already helping me be warmer in a cooler house. There are many good choices on Amazon, here’s one of them. Then pick out any USB battery pack to go with it, which also doubles as a very useful travel phone charger.

According to recent reports, having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

In a recent development, if you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That mentioned, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

You’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:.

Industry observers note that no matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data highlights the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

In a recent development, to save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

Other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

The next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment intends.

According to recent reports, if you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment plans and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

It has been revealed that once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

It has been revealed that then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

It’s vital to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as quickly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

Finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

Recent findings suggest that how much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete proposal that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

Focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

Buying a Duplex? Live in One Side to Put as Little as 3.5% Down

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lenders treat a duplex you live in as your home, so you can finance it with as little as 3.5% down on a government-insured FHA loan or 5% on a conventional loan.
  • Buy the same duplex as a rental you won’t live in, and an FHA loan, which the Federal Housing Administration insures, is off the table.
  • Industry observers note that FHA’s 3.5% minimum needs a credit score of 580 or higher, and scores from 500 to 579 need 10% down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lenders treat a duplex you live in as your home, so you can finance it with as little as 3.5% down on a government-insured FHA loan or 5% on a conventional loan. Buy one only if the other side’s rent, minus a quarter for repairs and empty months, leaves you paying less than a similar apartment rents for.

Buy the same duplex as a rental you won’t live in, and an FHA loan, which the Federal Housing Administration insures, is off the table. A conventional loan, one without government insurance, then takes 25% down.

Industry observers note that FHA’s 3.5% minimum needs a credit score of 580 or higher, and scores from 500 to 579 need 10% down. Freddie Mac, which buys many conventional loans from lenders, allows 5% down when its automated system approves the loan and the loan stays within a standard size limit, and 15% otherwise. Both loans require you to move in within 60 days and live there at least a year, after which you can move out and rent both sides.

In a recent development, either way, the lender counts 75% of the rent the other side is expected to bring when it decides whether you can afford the payment. Fannie Mae, the other significant buyer, counts it only if you already pay rent or own a home.

Say you put $12,600, or 3.5%, down on a $360,000 duplex, and your full payment, with taxes and insurance that covers the rented side, is $3,000 a month. The other side rents for $1,900, and a similar apartment would rent for $2,000. The tenant’s rent leaves you $1,100 to pay. Set aside a quarter of that rent, $475, for repairs and months the unit sits empty, and your side costs $1,575, or $425 less than the $2,000 apartment. A gap like that makes the duplex worth buying if you’re ready to live next to your tenant.

You’ll likely share a yard with your tenant, screen applicants, and take repair calls yourself. A duplex also draws fewer buyers than a single-family home when you sell. If those trade-offs outweigh the savings, there are other ways to cut your housing cost by renting out part of your home, from a spare room to a basement unit.

Get two numbers before you bid: what similar units nearby rent for, from current listings, and your full monthly payment, from a lender’s quote.

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

In a recent development, rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

According to recent reports, trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many owners like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Consumers who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

Recent findings suggest that pocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

It has been revealed that monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Owners often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Users who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

In a recent development, if you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused owners or those who prefer full manual control.

Subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android owners. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android people.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and strategy better for annual vs monthly charges.

Subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the federal tax credits that covered up to 30% of the cost of insulation, heat pumps, windows, and home solar ended for work installed after 2025.
  • In a recent development, the IRS ties the credits to the year the work was installed, not the year you paid, so a heat pump paid for in December 2025 and installed in January earns no credit.
  • In a recent development, many utilities still pay rebates on heat pumps and insulation, and some states offer their own tax credits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the federal tax credits that covered up to 30% of the cost of insulation, heat pumps, windows, and home solar ended for work installed after 2025. Before you sign a contract, check what your utility and your state will pay, since many rebates pay only if you apply first or use an approved contractor.

In a recent development, the IRS ties the credits to the year the work was installed, not the year you paid, so a heat pump paid for in December 2025 and installed in January earns no credit. Work installed by the end of 2025 still counts, and if your 2025 return left it out, you can claim it on an amended return with Form 5695 within three years of when you filed.

In a recent development, many utilities still pay rebates on heat pumps and insulation, and some states offer their own tax credits. Some state energy offices also run one or both federally funded Home Energy Rebates programs. One pays up to $4,000 toward a whole-home upgrade at any income, and more to lower-income households. The other pays up to $14,000 for electric upgrades like heat pumps to households earning up to 150% of their area’s median income, though no longer to replace gas or oil equipment.

In a recent development, the federal credits came at tax time, after the job. A rebate program may need to approve your project and your contractor before the work begins, and it pays only for equipment that meets its efficiency rules.

Industry observers note that search your ZIP code on DSIRE, NC State University’s database of state and utility incentives, and on ENERGY STAR’s Rebate Finder. Then check your utility’s rebates page, and ask your state energy office whether its programs have opened. A home energy audit from your utility can also point you to rebates.

According to recent reports, redo the payback, the years an upgrade’s savings take to cover its cost, counting only rebates you’ve confirmed. Say your utility’s rebate is the same as in 2025, a heat pump would have earned the full $2,000 credit, and it cuts your bills by $500 a year. It now costs you $2,000 more than it would have in 2025, which adds four years to its payback. That extra cost can put the cheap upgrades that pay back fastest ahead of big projects.

Before you sign, ask the contractor which of these programs it’s enrolled in, and get any approval a rebate requires in writing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your 401(k) contribution limit starts over on January 1, and any room you don’t use by your last December paycheck is gone for good.
  • Industry observers note that doing this every January matters because the limit moves.
  • According to recent reports, the limit counts contributions by calendar year, and every dollar has to come out of that year’s paychecks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your 401(k) contribution limit starts over on January 1, and any room you don’t use by your last December paycheck is gone for good. Each January, look up the upcoming IRS limit, divide it by your number of paychecks, and set your contribution to that amount if your budget allows.

Industry observers note that doing this every January matters because the limit moves. The IRS adjusts it for inflation, and when it rises, a per-paycheck amount that maxed you out last year leaves room unused.

According to recent reports, the limit counts contributions by calendar year, and every dollar has to come out of that year’s paychecks. It’s also a limit per person, not per job. If you switched employers this year, what went into the old initiative counts too, and keeping the combined total under the limit is on you.

To hit the max from any point in the year, take the current limit, subtract what you’ve already contributed, and divide by the paychecks you have left. Enter that as a dollar amount, or convert it to a percentage of your pay. If you’ll be 50 or older by December 31 and your plan offers catch-up contributions, you can add one on top, with a larger allowance in the years you turn 60 through 63. In a plan with a Roth option, the IRS requires the catch-up to go in as Roth, taxed now instead of at withdrawal, if your wages from that employer topped the high-earner threshold the year before.

Spread your contributions across the whole year if your employer matches each paycheck. Hit the limit by summer and the later paychecks can go unmatched, unless your plan makes up the difference with a year-end true-up. Ask HR which kind you have.

In a recent development, if you changed jobs, add up both intends before you set the fresh rate. Any excess has to come out by April 15 of the following year, or it’s taxed twice, once for the year you contributed it and again when you withdraw it.

Industry observers note that contribute at least enough to collect your whole employer match if the full limit is out of reach. Then put part of every pay raise toward a higher rate. Your take-home pay still grows, and contributions that rise faster than the limit shrink the gap to the max.

Sources indicate that in 2008, as stocks crashed, the average value of U.S. farm real estate fell just 3.2%, its first drop since 1987, USDA reported. Its Land Values 2026 Summary shows only two dips since 2012, both about 0.3%.

It has been revealed that cash rent on U.S. cropland averaged $160 an acre in 2026, about 2.7% of the average acre’s $6,020 value, by the Economic Research Service’s figures. The rest of the return comes from the land’s price, which moves with crop prices and interest rates and can stall. Cropland gained 3.3% in 2026, but 0.3% after inflation.

Only two farmland real estate investment trusts trade publicly, Farmland Partners and Gladstone Land, and you can hold either in any brokerage account or IRA. Expect a bumpier ride than USDA’s numbers show, since the shares are priced every trading day while USDA’s land values come from a once-a-year survey of farm operators.

Industry observers note that platforms such as AcreTrader and FarmTogether sell stakes in single farms, but only to accredited investors. To qualify under SEC rules, you need a net worth over $1 million outside your home, or income over $200,000 ($300,000 for a couple) in each of the past two years and expected this year. Minimums are usually $15,000 or more, fees vary by deal, neither platform offers a resale market, and AcreTrader puts typical holds at five to 10 years. For most investors, a REIT is a better start than a platform deal.

Say you want 5% of a $500,000 portfolio, or $25,000, in farmland. In a single almond orchard deal, that money depends on one farm’s water supply and harvests for a decade. In a farmland REIT in your IRA, it’s spread across more than 140 farms, and you can sell any trading day.

Industry observers note that the SEC states REIT dividends are usually taxed at your regular income rate. Hold the REIT in an IRA, where they aren’t taxed as they’re paid, and keep farmland near 5% of your portfolio.

Industry observers note that managing money as a household is harder than it looks. Most people use a regular checking account at a big bank, then juggle a separate budgeting app, maybe a savings account somewhere else, and possibly a kids’ debit card on top of that. It’s a lot to keep track of.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features – all inside a single app. The goal is to help you organize your money, automate your budget, and earn more interest without switching between apps.

In this Crew review, we cover what it is, how it works, who it’s best for, the key features, pricing, and what real users are saying. If you’re looking for a smarter checking account that does more, this review gives you the full picture.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features.

Crew is a financial technology (fintech) company based in Lehi, Utah. It was founded by Gentry Davies and Steve Domino, who previously worked at Divvy, a business expense platform acquired by Bill.com. The app introduced publicly and has been growing steadily since 2023.

Crew is not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, which is FDIC-insured. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are protected up to federal insurance limits – $250,000 for individual accounts and $500,000 for joint accounts.

It has been revealed that the app is available on both iOS and Android. A web app is presently in beta.

Crew offers a checking account that earns 2.95% APY on your full balance. This rate applies to every dollar you hold in the account – there’s no minimum deposit requirement and no tiered rate structure.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Most significant bank checking accounts pay close to 0.01% APY. Earning nearly 3% on your everyday checking balance can add meaningful interest over time, especially for families keeping a few thousand dollars in their account at any given time.

Recent findings suggest that pockets are virtual “buckets” inside your single Crew checking account. You can create as many as you need – for example, one for bills, one for savings, one for a vacation fund, one for groceries.

Why it matters: You don’t need a separate savings account or multiple bank accounts. Pockets let you visually and mentally divide your money without moving it to another institution. You can also lock a pocket in “piggy bank mode” to avoid dipping into it.

Sources indicate that crew’s Autopilot feature lets you create rules that move money automatically based on triggers. Triggers can be events like a paycheck arriving or a balance dropping below a set level, or they can be time-based, like every Friday or the 1st of the month.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Automation removes the discipline requirement from budgeting. You set your rules once, and Crew handles the rest. For example, you can tell Crew to automatically send 10% of every paycheck to your giving pocket, $500 to bills, and keep the rest in checking — without touching the app every payday.

Why it matters: Most banking apps bolt on a kid’s account as an afterthought. Crew builds family banking into the core experience. Parents get real-time spending notifications, spend controls, and the ability to set automated allowances.

Industry observers note that parents can set up automatic recurring transfers to a child’s account. You define the amount and the schedule, and Crew handles the delivery.

Why it matters: Automated allowances teach kids about money while removing the “I forgot to pay your allowance” problem for parents. Kids learn what consistent saving looks like in practice.

According to recent reports, every account member gets a Mastercard debit card. You can switch which pocket your card draws from at any time inside the app – or update a transaction after the fact if you accidentally spent from the wrong pocket.

According to recent reports, why it matters: This setup means budgeting is “baked in” to your spending. Instead of tracking what you spent after the fact, you decide which budget category you’re spending from before or at the time of purchase.

You can use your Crew Mastercard at any ATM in the Mastercard, Maestro, or Cirrus networks. Crew does not have its own fee-free ATM network, but it reimburses ATM fees for up to 20 withdrawals per year.

Why it matters: The annual ATM fee reimbursement covers most casual cash users without adding much complexity.

Crew supports outgoing wire transfers. The fee depends on your total account balance.

Industry observers note that have the money conversation with your aging parents while everyone is healthy, not in a hospital hallway. You don’t need their net worth. You need to know where the documents are, who their advisors are, what insurance they carry, and whether a power of attorney exists.

Too often, this talk happens after a fall or a stroke, when nobody can find anything.

It has been revealed that picture a daughter whose father is in intensive care. His mortgage is due, his bank won’t discuss his accounts with her, and no one knows which company holds his life insurance. With no power of attorney on file, paying his bills may mean going to court.

Avoiding that can take one uncomfortable afternoon, and the list is shorter than you might fear. You aren’t asking what your parents are worth, the question that makes the talk feel like an audit. You’re asking what’s in place, where it is, and who handles it:.

It has been revealed that open with your own planning instead of theirs. Say you just named someone to make medical decisions for you and realized you don’t know what they’ve set up. A friend’s parent getting sick works, too. Let them decide how much to share and who takes each role.

Recent findings suggest that be ready for two hard truths. The money may be thinner than you assumed, so listen rather than judge. And trouble can show up first as money problems. The National Institute on Aging states money problems may be among the earliest signs of dementia, such as unpaid bills or a burst of newly introduced purchases, and scammers target older adults. People 60 and older reported more than $7.7 billion in fraud losses to the FBI in 2025.

The money stays theirs, and so do the choices. Your part is making sure that if someone ever has to act for them, it’s the person they picked, doing what they asked.

#79629. What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Wellkeptwallet ↗ Open Full Page

What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

📅 07 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone.
  • Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table.
  • In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

Dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

The result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

In a recent development, most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

Industry observers note that because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

For most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

Recent findings suggest that say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:.

Recent findings suggest that after three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

In a recent development, this is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

It removes emotion from investing.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

It makes market downturns work for you.

When markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

It is accessible no matter your income.

You do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

According to recent reports, want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

According to recent reports, if you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single company’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small.

Sources indicate that things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market.

Industry observers note that research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That mentioned, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Recent findings suggest that getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:.

Dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

The key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

Latest Update: What Are Mutual Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list.
  • This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.
  • A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

It has been revealed that each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Recent findings suggest that mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

It has been revealed that when you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

Sources indicate that investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund firm or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

Recent findings suggest that these funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds (fixed income funds).

According to recent reports, bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

It has been revealed that these funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Recent findings suggest that money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most key things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

The problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

Sources indicate that for most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Sources indicate that fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Sources indicate that some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

These are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

Recent findings suggest that when you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

For investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Sources indicate that most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly.

This is the biggest issue with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

In a recent development, when a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an matter in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

Sources indicate that it is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

It has been revealed that with thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Industry observers note that mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

It has been revealed that that said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most notable step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

House Flipping Profit Starts With Your Offer – Cap It With the 70% Rule

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that before you bid on a house to flip, cap your offer at 70% of its expected sale price after repairs, minus the repair budget.
  • In the second quarter of 2026, the typical flipped home sold for $60,526 more than the flipper paid, before renovation or any other cost, property data firm ATTOM reports.
  • Recent findings suggest that the 70% rule caps that purchase price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that before you bid on a house to flip, cap your offer at 70% of its expected sale price after repairs, minus the repair budget. The other 30% has to cover the loan, the bills while you own it, and the cost of selling, so every dollar you pay above the cap comes out of your profit.

In the second quarter of 2026, the typical flipped home sold for $60,526 more than the flipper paid, before renovation or any other cost, property data firm ATTOM reports. The market sets the sale price, so most flips are won or lost at the purchase.

Recent findings suggest that the 70% rule caps that purchase price. Start with the after-repair value, what the house should sell for once it’s fixed, based on recent sales of similar updated homes nearby. Multiply it by 70%, then subtract a detailed repair estimate with 10% to 20% added for surprises. That’s your highest offer, not your target.

The loan, the holding costs while you own the house, and the selling costs come out of the other 30%. Private lenders’ short-term loans to real estate investors, often called hard money loans, charged a median 9.99% interest rate in October 2026, plus up-front fees of 1.75% of the loan, the National Private Lenders Association reports. Holding costs are property taxes, insurance, and utilities, and selling costs are agent commissions and closing costs.

In a recent development, say a house should sell for $300,000 after a $40,000 renovation, with $35,000 in loan, holding, and selling costs. Seventy percent of $300,000 is $210,000, so subtracting the renovation caps your offer at $170,000. At that price, $55,000 is left before income tax. Pay $230,000 instead, and you’d lose at least $5,000, since a bigger loan costs more interest.

Sources indicate that sell within a year of buying, and the IRS taxes the profit as a short-term capital gain, at the same rates as your wages. Once flipping becomes your business, the profit is business income instead, which also owes self-employment tax for Social Security and Medicare.

Recent findings suggest that the typical flip in ATTOM’s report took 161 days from purchase to resale. A slow permit or a late contractor adds weeks or months of interest and holding costs, and a cooling market can cut the sale price.

Get an agent’s list of recent sales and a contractor’s written estimate before you bid, then write your cap down. Walk away from any house whose seller won’t come down to it.
